questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: Linear approximation from a tangent line
questions.learningObjective: Apply a tangent-line linear approximation to estimate a nearby function value.
questions.stem: A graph of f shows a tangent line touching the curve at x = 2, where the curve reads 7 and the slope is 3. Estimate f(2.1) from the graph alone.

options.text: About 7.3, obtained by adding the slope times 0.1 to the value read at the point of tangency.
About 7.0, because the tangent line keeps the same height as the curve at the touch point.
options.misconception: thinks the tangent value holds constant for all nearby x

options.text: About 7.1, because only one tenth of the slope should be added to the value at the touch point.
options.misconception: divides the slope by the step size instead of multiplying

options.text: About 10.3, because the slope should be added to the value at the origin before shifting x.
options.misconception: anchors the tangent line at the origin, not the touch point

questions.explanation: Linear approximation gives f(2.1) = 7 + 3(0.1) = 7.3. The tangent matches the curve only at the touch point, so 7 alone is not the estimate and the origin plays no part in a local model.
questions.hint: Add the slope times the step to the tangent value.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: The second-order Taylor approximation
questions.learningObjective: Compute a second-order Taylor approximation from readings taken off a graph.
questions.stem: Near x = 3, a graph of f gives readings f(3) = 4, f'(3) = 2 and f''(3) = 6. What does the second-order approximation at x = 3 give for f(3.1)?
questions.explanation: The second-order formula adds the curvature term, so the estimate is 4 + 2(0.1) + 3(0.1)^2 = 4.23. Omitting the quadratic term would give only 4.2, and doubling the curvature contribution would give 4.26.
questions.hint: Include the half-curvature term with the squared step.

options.text: Replace x by 0.6, since the series was written about a = 2 and the shift is already built in.
options.misconception: subtracts the centre from x yet keeps the (x - 2) factors

options.text: Replace x by 2.6 and evaluate each (x - 2) factor at 0.6, since the series is in powers of x - 2.
Replace x by 2.6 and evaluate each (x - 2) factor at 2.6, since the factor equals the argument.
options.misconception: reads (x - 2) as the whole argument x, not a shift

questions.explanation: A Taylor series about a = 2 is written in powers of (x - 2), so each factor uses the shift 0.6. Reducing x but keeping the factors, or keeping the factors at the full x, both describe a different series.

options.misconception: believes a series can only match at its centre point

options.text: For all x, since the graph is smooth except at one isolated asymptote.
options.misconception: ignores that the series fails to converge past the asymptote

options.text: For x greater than 3 only, since the graph is smooth everywhere to the right.
options.misconception: confuses graph smoothness with actual series convergence

options.text: For -3 < x < 3, since the nearest singularity to the centre sits at distance 3.

options.misconception: assumes a higher degree always clears the accuracy threshold

options.misconception: credits the constant term with describing the curvature

options.text: The term f'(a)(x - a), which bends the straight line into the parabola on the graph.
options.misconception: credits the linear term with producing the curvature

options.text: The term one half of f''(a)(x - a) squared, which bends the line into the drawn curve.
No term, since a second-order approximation stays a straight line and shows no curvature.
options.misconception: believes truncation order cannot change the shape

options.misconception: adds the centre instead of subtracting it

5, because the asymptote at x = -5 is the one whose distance was noticed first on the graph.
options.misconception: picks the first asymptote seen rather than the closest one

options.text: 2.61, because the second derivative must be doubled before being applied.
options.misconception: doubles the curvature term instead of halving it

questions.hint: The curvature term carries a factor of one half.

options.misconception: compares the wrong pair of degrees for the stated gain

options.text: Degree 3 is worse than degree 2, because the last error is the smallest but least reliable.

The error is still far too large, because 0.0018 is larger than 0.001 by a wide margin.

questions.topic: Linear approximation from a tangent line
questions.learningObjective: Justify using a tangent line to estimate a nearby function value.
questions.stem: A tangent drawn at the point x = 2 sits on a graph of f. Which statement explains why the tangent is used to estimate f nearby?

options.text: Because the tangent is the curve with its curvature removed, so it can never be wrong.
options.misconception: claims the tangent model is error free

options.text: Because the tangent is the shortest path between two marked points on the graph.
options.misconception: misdescribes the tangent as a shortest path

options.text: Because the tangent's slope equals the average rate of change over the whole plotted window.
options.misconception: confuses the derivative with an average rate

options.text: Because it matches both the value and the slope at the point, so the first error is small.

questions.explanation: The tangent reproduces f and f' at the tangency point, and the first neglected term grows with the square of the step, so nearby estimates are good. Its slope is a local rate, not an average.
questions.hint: A local model matches height and steepness at one point.

questions.topic: The second-order Taylor approximation
questions.learningObjective: Compare a second-order model with the graph on one side of the centre.
questions.stem: A second-order model where the curvature is positive is fitted at a centre a of a graph. How does the model sit relative to the graph just right of a?

options.text: Below the graph, because a positive curvature pulls the modelled curve downward.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of a positive curvature

options.text: Above the graph, because a positive curvature bends the modelled parabola upward.
Exactly on the graph, because the second-order term is fitted to the local bend.
options.misconception: believes matching the curvature reproduces the curve

options.text: Either side, depending on whether the step is taken to the right or the left.
options.misconception: claims the side depends on the direction of the step

questions.explanation: A positive second derivative bends the modelled parabola upward, so to the right of the centre it rides above a concave-up curve. It copies the local bend only, and the side does not flip with the step.
questions.hint: Think of the parabola bending the same way as the graph.

questions.topic: Taylor series about a non-zero centre
questions.learningObjective: Extract the slope at the centre from a table of series coefficients.
questions.stem: A table of coefficients under a graph of f lists each power of (x - 3) for an expansion about a = 3. What does it allow you to read directly?

options.text: The slope of the graph at the centre, taken from the coefficient of the first power.
The value of the graph at the origin of the axes, from the constant coefficient.
options.misconception: reads the constant term as the value at the axis origin

options.text: The curvature of the graph at the far right end of the plotted window.
options.misconception: reads a local coefficient as a value at the window edge

options.text: The distance from the centre to the nearest singularity shown on the graph.
options.misconception: reads a coefficient as a distance to a singularity

questions.explanation: The coefficient of the first power of (x - 3) is f'(3), so the table gives the slope at the centre directly. The constant term gives f(3), and no coefficient encodes a distance to a singularity.
questions.hint: The first power of the shifted factor carries the slope.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: The radius of convergence is set by the nearest singularity
questions.learningObjective: Decide which fact settles whether a series can be used on a short interval.
questions.stem: A series needed only between x = -1 and x = 1 is expanded about a = 0, while the graph shows a vertical asymptote at x = 6. Which fact is decisive?

options.text: The asymptote at x = 6, because it is the only blow-up point visible anywhere near.
options.misconception: fixes on a singularity outside the region of use

options.text: Nothing, because the interval of use lies inside the radius, so the asymptote is irrelevant.
options.misconception: calls the singularity irrelevant instead of measuring the radius

options.text: The radius is at least 1, since the interval of use sits within the distance to the asymptote.
The asymptote at x = 6 gives radius 6, so the interval of use is certainly covered.
options.misconception: assumes convergence inside the radius is guaranteed

questions.explanation: The nearest singularity is 6 units from the centre, so the radius is at least 6 and the interval from -1 to 1 lies well inside it. The region of use must be nearer the centre than any singularity.
questions.hint: Check the distance from the centre to the nearest singularity.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the practice that makes a truncation-error table useful.
questions.stem: A table of truncation errors by degree is printed under a graph of a function. Which practice makes the table genuinely useful?

options.text: Using the table only to confirm that the plotted curve is smooth near the expansion point.
options.misconception: uses the table as a smoothness check only

options.text: Choosing the degree that produces the most terms in the printed expansion.
options.misconception: maximises the number of terms rather than accuracy

options.text: Ignoring the table when the graph already looks smooth to the eye.
options.misconception: trusts the eye over the measured errors

options.text: Matching the tabulated error to the accuracy the task actually needs before choosing.

questions.explanation: The table is measured error data, so it helps when each entry is compared with the accuracy the task demands and the least sufficient degree is chosen. Using it to comment on smoothness wastes it.
